lead.t: Gastroschisis has no sac, is right of the cord and has few associated anomalies other than atresia.
lead.s: Congenital Abdominal Wall Defects: Umbilical Hernia, Omphalocele and Gastroschis

b: Definition. A full-thickness defect of the abdominal wall, usually to the right of a normal umbilical cord , through which bowel herniates. There is no sac , and no liver or spleen outside the abdomen.
Thought to be due to an ischaemic event (disruption of the right omphalomesenteric artery) or rupture of an embryonic omphalocele in utero.
Loops of small and large bowel are exposed to amniotic fluid, so they are thickened, matted together and covered with a shaggy inflammatory "peel" . The bowel looks short.
Associated anomalies are uncommon (under 10%). The exception is intestinal atresia (from infarction of herniated bowel) and malrotation (non-rotation of the midgut is always present).
More than 70% of babies are premature or small for dates. It is more common in babies of young mothers.

snip.t: A gastroschisis is an anterior abdominal wall defect that lies lateral to the umbilicus and has no covering.

Associated conditions: heterotaxy syndromes, congenital diaphragmatic hernia, abdominal wall defects (gastroschisis, exomphalos), duodenal and jejunal atresia, Hirschsprung's, intestinal atresia, cardiac anomalies, and Down syndrome.

snip.t: Associated conditions: hypospadias, patent processus vaginalis (inguinal hernia), abdominal wall defects (prune belly, gastroschisis, omphalocele), cerebral palsy, Wilms tumour, syndromes such as Klinefelter's, and hypogonadotropic hypogonadism.
Covered by a peritoneal/amniotic sac (unlike gastroschisis, which has no covering sac)
Gastroschisis — herniation of abdominal contents through an abdominal wall defect, without a covering sac

es.q: Discuss the rotation of the midgut and associated congenital anomalies like omphalocele and gastroschisis.
es.m:
- **Midgut rotation**: 90° counter‑clockwise during herniation → 180° additional rotation after return to abdomen → total 270°.
- **Omphalocele**: failure of the midgut to return → abdominal contents herniate into umbilical cord; often associated with other anomalies.
- **Gastroschisis**: defect in the abdominal wall lateral to the umbilicus → intestines herniate without covering sac.
- **Clinical relevance**: requires surgical repair; associated with intestinal malrotation and volvulus.
